History & Culture

Japan put the originals on display. A century looks different on paper.

The second half of “Memories of Showa Diplomacy” opens today. Treaties and records turn a familiar timeline back into decisions preserved in ink.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
October 14, 2026 · 20:30 JST

A treaty is easy to flatten into a date. In Tokyo’s Diplomatic Archives it becomes an object again: paper chosen by officials, language negotiated across governments, seals attached to authority and a record carried through a century that repeatedly changed Japan’s place in the world.

Today the Foreign Ministry opened the second display period of Memories of Showa Diplomacy. It marks 100 years since 1926, the first Showa year, and runs at Azabudai Hills’ Mori JP Tower through November 28, 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. The first period ended October 10; the objects have changed.

One era, several Japans

Showa extended into January 1989. It contained militarism, war and defeat; occupation and a new constitution; rapid growth; Cold War alliances; normalization and wider international engagement. Rotating fragile originals protects them, but also resists the idea that one object can represent 64 years.

The ministry calls the exhibition a chance to consider the foundations of peaceful postwar Japan. That is an official framing, not the only interpretation. Careful viewing asks who authored each record, whose voice is absent and how later events changed its meaning.

1926First Showa year.
64 yearsThe era’s span.
Nov. 28Second period ends.

A scan can transmit every word. The physical page reveals scale and bureaucracy: where a signature sits, how parties share space and whether an object was made for ceremony or work. Diplomacy appears as labor before it becomes memory.

How to read the room

Begin with the date, then separate signing from implementation. Identify the parties and form—treaty, note, memorandum or internal record. Check which languages carry authority. Finally ask what happened next. An agreement records a moment; it does not guarantee how people experienced it.

The Japanese word 史料, shiryō, means historical source material. 史 is history; 料 is material. It is evidence from which history is constructed, not history already finished.

Why today?

The history is not new. Access is. A different group of original materials became available today after the exhibition’s intermission. Visitors should confirm opening days and photography conditions before traveling to 1-3-1 Azabudai, Minato-ku.

The reason to go is not nostalgia but friction. An original puts a signature where a textbook gives a sentence and shows that today’s Japan emerged from specific choices rather than a smooth national story.
